knowledge: The book’s theme is back office (バックオフィス), covering accounting/finance (経理), human resources (人事), legal (法務), and general affairs (総務), and it explains those functions and the actual work involved.
Primary readers are people who do back-office work themselves and people who are building a back-office organization; it is aimed at beginners through intermediate practitioners.

Goals for newly assigned staff: understand what work they should actually do. Goals for small or one-person back offices: get a complete, leak-free view of required work and the overall picture when one person covers many areas.
The book stresses a whole-back-office viewpoint and the value the function provides, not only specialist knowledge in each silo (accounting, HR, legal, etc.).

It also aims to give back-office people a sense of experience and growth, and to help executives and other departments understand back office so they can build the organization and relationships better.
Content is designed to cover basic operations comprehensively so that as much work as possible can be handled in-house, even though some companies outsource parts of back office to specialists.

A distinctive feature is treating back office as one function rather than isolated domains: finding common threads across management/back-office departments and sending messages that apply to everyone who works there. Specialist books already exist for each single area.

Author self-introduction: Yusuke Uenishi (植西祐介), qualified as certified public accountant (公認会計士), tax accountant (税理士), and social insurance and labor consultant (社会保険労務士); representative of Conduct Group.

Conduct Group is a cluster of a management consulting firm, an accounting office, and a social insurance labor consultant office that together offer one-stop back-office support, from startups to large companies and from traditional to cutting-edge businesses.

Author background: new-graduate hire in the management department of a listed chemical manufacturer, accumulating experience in corporate planning (経営企画) and accounting/finance (経理) at both headquarters and factory sites, representing traditional Japanese large-enterprise management practice.
While working at a manufacturer factory, the author passed the Japanese CPA (公認会計士) exam, then joined a major audit firm performing financial statement audits and internal-control audits.

After audit experience, the author moved into management consulting, working at an audit-firm-group comprehensive consulting company and a foreign strategy consulting firm, later serving as CFO and corporate-office head at a startup that scaled from single-digit employees (zero-to-one phase) to over 100 people, covering broad back-office operations and management.

Career spans large enterprises, SMEs, and startups; functional domains include corporate planning, accounting, HR, legal, and general affairs; combined internal-practitioner and external-professional/consultant perspectives.

This hybrid, wide-ranging practical experience in back-office domains is presented as the basis for problem-solving capability; like-minded colleagues later formed the professional firm Conduct Group.

Back-office functions (経理, 人事, etc.) are typically not a company’s core departments; if management functions themselves become the core that drives the company, it can be a warning sign that actual business activities may not be progressing well.

Common complaints other departments voice about back office, based on the author’s extensive company experience: “It’s clerical work anyone can do, no pressure, looks easy”; “We can’t see what work they actually do and don’t understand it”; “They don’t understand the field/business side”; “They only say rigid or conservative things”; “They generate no sales, only costs.”
Back offices are often undervalued because they are not fulfilling (or not perceived as fulfilling) the functions they originally should have.
The key solution keyword for raising back-office standing is 'connection with management' (経営との接続).

The definition of back office is broad; its highest roles include CFO (Chief Financial Officer) and CHRO (Chief Human Resources Officer), whose necessity is increasing year by year. Some companies now also appoint CLO (Chief Legal Officer) and CAO (Chief Administrative Officer).
CXO-level back-office leaders typically started as individual-contributor players; the difference is involvement in management (経営への関与).
A CFO's mission is to optimize company-wide allocation of financial resources from a finance perspective, using strategic methods such as M&A.
A CHRO's mission is to build an organization that produces the strongest performance by driving system design, hiring, and culture creation.
High value is created precisely because the work is tied to strategy and management.

Back-office work is actually difficult to replace. In newly founded small companies, the president or close relatives typically handle front-office work while also performing accounting, hiring, and other back-office tasks.
Casually handing back-office work to someone else can immediately make important numbers invisible or hinder organization-building.
Selecting who will be entrusted with back-office work is originally an extremely important decision.
True back-office work is an act of handing over part of the 'company management control' that the founder/manager values with their lifeblood; the responsibility is heavy and expectations are high.

Therefore the essence and true mission of back-office work should be understanding the manager's intent and running operations from the same viewpoint—i.e., 'connection with the manager.' This is the book's central theme.
Raising the value of the back-office function is both the author's company mission and personal life's work.
バックオフィス (back office) とは、経理・人事・総務・法務といった業務を総称した部署や業務のことであり、「管理部門」「間接部門」「コーポレート部門」とも呼ばれる。
営業部門や開発部門はフロントオフィス（フロント業務）と呼ばれ、バックオフィスはそれと対比される会社の裏方の仕事を行う部署を指す。
フロントオフィス側の機能例には販売、アフターサービス、企画・開発、製造、物流、マーケティング、サービスがあり、これらをバックオフィスが支える関係にある。

Back office operations (バックオフィス業務) have three main characteristics: (1) a higher proportion of routine/standardized work than non-routine work; (2) work that requires specialized knowledge such as laws and accounting rules; (3) work that governs company-wide management control (経営管理).
Back office tasks are frequently performed in aggregated time units such as daily, weekly, monthly, or yearly rather than as one-off activities.

Payment processing example: the back-office staff receives invoices from suppliers at the beginning of the month, compiles a list of amounts to be paid that month, executes bank transfers at month-end, and records the payment results in the accounting books. Despite variations in invoice content or payees, this is a recurring monthly routine.

Because much back-office work is repetitive, many companies hire clerical staff (事務職) specialized in administrative processing and create dedicated departments so that routine tasks can be performed repeatedly and efficiency can be improved.

Back-office work requires knowledge of the laws and rules that govern company management, including the Companies Act (会社法), labor law, tax law, accounting standards, bookkeeping, talent management, and business models.
The required knowledge is at the level expected of company executives; genuine task execution is impossible without absorbing and understanding this knowledge.
The relevant knowledge is not static: laws and rules change every year, so practitioners must continually update themselves.
Because the volume of required knowledge is vast, some tasks cannot be covered by an individual or by the company alone; specialists in each back-office domain should therefore be utilized.
Back-office work is not merely an administrative-processing function; it is the function that governs company-wide management control.
The value back office should deliver is supporting management decision-making from the three perspectives of people, goods, and money (ヒト・モノ・カネ) and guiding the organization toward problem-solving.

While the front office builds the business day by day, the back office analyzes from a company-wide viewpoint that the front office cannot see, supplies information to the front office and management, identifies current issues, and jointly solves those issues with a future-oriented view.

Back office cannot function in isolation. As a management-control function it must constantly survey the entire company and consider what must be done for both short-term and long-term corporate development.
Personnel who correctly understand these three characteristics of back-office work and can embody them in daily activity are actually scarce.

From the early 2010s through the following decade, digitalization has been an unavoidable, large-scale transformation in the back-office domain, creating a strong need for corresponding change in back-office talent.

Traditional Japanese companies often positioned back-office operations primarily as a group performing standardized routine/clerical transactional processing, with insufficient specialized knowledge and management-control functions that back-office should originally possess.
This traditional tendency is being disrupted by recent environmental changes; one major trend is the digitalization and DX (Digital Transformation) of back-office operations.
Digitalization of back-office work is described as urgent ('no waiting' / 待ったなし).
A major change from digitalization is that tasks previously possible only through manual labor can now be automatically processed by systems.
Automatic processing is enabled by standardizing business flows and having systems memorize them, via RPA (Robotic Process Automation: ロボティクス・プロセス・オートメーション).
Data import combined with image recognition via OCR (Optical Character Recognition) or AI learning can greatly reduce the labor of data input.
RPA, OCR, and AI-related functions for automating and simplifying back-office work are rapidly spreading and penetrating organizations.
Back-office operations encompass accounting, human resources (人事), legal affairs (法務), general affairs (総務), management planning (経営企画), and DX (digital transformation).

RPA (Robotic Process Automation) automates repetitive data-handling workflows that previously required human steps: searching for data, downloading/dropping data, inputting data, and processing/analyzing data.
Once an RPA program is started, it automatically executes the full sequence of those data tasks (labeled ①–④ in the typical flow) without further human intervention.

OCR (Optical Character Recognition) converts paper documents into usable digital text: a smartphone or scanner first turns the paper into image data, after which AI automatically identifies and extracts the characters from that image.
Together, RPA and OCR form core automation techniques for digitizing and streamlining traditional paper-based or manual back-office processes.

Traditional corporate back-office systems were often heavily customized, rigid, and required company-specific processing, so they demanded high operator skill and were sometimes unusable by ordinary back-office staff.

Modern cloud-type back-office systems emphasize UI/UX (user experience, visibility, and ease of use) and typically include API (Application Programming Interface) linkage as a standard feature, making inter-system data integration more efficient and reducing the need to operate complex custom systems.
Back-office work can no longer avoid systems: most of the clerical/transaction-processing functions the back office previously performed are being replaced by systems.
Digitalization greatly reduces human data-entry work that clerical staff used to do, making much of that labor unnecessary.
To survive as both a company and as individuals amid digital change, back-office staff must become people who can master and fully utilize systems rather than only perform clerical tasks.

System skills required of a digitally transforming back office include: understanding the purposes the company wants to achieve through DX; reorganizing existing routine work and considering what can be systematized; being able to compare and evaluate commercially available systems and their functions; being able to drive system implementation as the responsible staff member; knowing internal processing and master-data design mechanisms; and being able to collaborate with vendors and internal IT on error handling.
Back-office professionals do not need skills to build or modify systems themselves, because system development is not their core job.
To master systems, it is essential to understand the relationship between inputs (what is entered) and outputs (how processing actually behaves as a result).
Back-office DX (digital transformation) requires an accurate understanding of systems, not only operational knowledge.
The basic flow of any system is Input (情報の入力) → internal processing by predetermined rules/methods → Output (処理結果).
Understanding a system means knowing: what information must be entered, what processing the system then performs, and what results it produces.
Details of back-office DX are covered in Chapter 7 of the source book.
Back-office work cannot be performed without understanding laws and rules (法令・ルール).

Legal affairs (法務) must understand many laws, including the Companies Act (会社法), Antimonopoly Act (独占禁止法), Subcontract Act (下請法), Act against Unjustifiable Premiums and Misleading Representations (景品表示法), and Patent Act (特許法).
Legal understanding is required even for non-legal back-office functions.
Accounting (経理) requires understanding of tax law (税法) and accounting standards (会計基準) to perform proper accounting treatment and tax filings.

Human resources (人事) requires understanding of labor laws such as the Labor Standards Act (労働基準法) and Labor Contract Act (労働契約法), plus social-insurance laws including the Health Insurance Act (健康保険法) and Employees' Pension Insurance Act (厚生年金保険法).
Management planning (経営企画) for new businesses may involve industry-specific legal systems of the new field of entry.
A core environmental pressure on back offices is responding to repeated legal amendments and maintaining awareness of legal compliance (法令遵守).
The number of laws that back-office functions must grasp is very large.

Back-office work (accounting, HR/labor, legal, general affairs, management planning, and DX) requires knowledge of a large number of Japanese laws and rules in order to support business operations and management.

Core statutes and rules frequently relevant to back office include accounting standards, the Labor Standards Act, Companies Act, Corporate Tax Act, Industrial Safety and Health Act, Antimonopoly Act, Consumption Tax Act, Insurance Act, Patent Act, Income Tax Act, Trademark Act, Local Tax Act, Stamp Tax Act, Act against Unjustifiable Premiums and Misleading Representations, Financial Instruments and Exchange Act, Childcare and Family Care Leave Act, Subcontract Act, and Worker Dispatching Act.
Back-office staff must use this legal knowledge for risk management in business development and corporate management.
Ongoing duties include responding to legal amendments and ensuring legal compliance (コンプライアンス).
Laws (法令) are amended frequently, almost every year, and back-office operations have a very close relationship with laws; legal changes have a large impact on back-office work.
Proceeding with only a shallow understanding of laws can easily lead to unintentional legal violations (法令違反).
The importance of legal compliance (法令遵守 / コンプライアンス) has been increasing year by year.
In an era when corporate scandals spread easily via SNS, legal violations now tend to cause much larger losses to companies than before.

Back-office staff must perform appropriate legal risk management through these actions: (1) build a mechanism to regularly collect law-related back-office information; (2) collaborate with domain experts (lawyers, tax accountants, certified public accountants, social insurance labor consultants, patent attorneys, etc.) to keep information up to date; (3) correctly evaluate the impact of legal or institutional changes on the company; (4) consider countermeasures such as forming projects according to the degree of impact; (5) involve appropriate internal parties (front-line departments, management, etc.) and communicate legal information.
Recent digital-environment change and rising legal-understanding requirements have gradually raised the performance standard expected of back-office functions.
Highly specialized back-office talent does not appear overnight simply because the environment changed; required people remain in short supply at first.

One structural cause of shortage is talent ‘fixing’: back-office staff typically have low turnover and long tenure because work is easily standardized and routinized; longer tenure further optimizes processes, so companies can run operations with fewer people and lower cost.
Firms therefore postpone talent refresh, while employees accept the role for stable (if not high) income.
Low labor-market liquidity and little inflow of new people mean the quality of candidates circulating in the market does not improve.
Historically the back-office talent market was not characterized by high quality or high compensation.

Rapid environmental change produces a large mismatch: companies now need higher work and skill levels (including IT literacy) than they previously demanded, while employment conditions (starting with salary) have not kept pace.
Consequently, people who can cover accounting, HR, legal and related domains at the newly required breadth and IT-literacy level are scarce, and the overall talent market is in supply shortage.

There is a mismatch in the back-office talent market: roles often offer relatively stable conditions and treatment, while available people may only have executed assigned tasks rather than independently running operations with IT literacy and knowledge.
One solution under talent shortage is using BPO (Business Process Outsourcing) providers and specialists. BPO means outsourcing part of a company’s business processes.

More companies now offer back-office BPO. Accounting (経理) and HR/labor (人事労務) in particular have relatively many tasks that are easy to outsource, so firms often supplement missing headcount from outside when they cannot hire.

Back-office domains have many licensed specialists: lawyers (弁護士) and patent attorneys (弁理士) for legal; tax accountants (税理士) and certified public accountants (公認会計士) for accounting; labor and social security attorneys (社会保険労務士) for labor/HR.
Back-office operations (バックオフィス業務) span accounting (経理), HR/labor (人事労務), legal (法務), general affairs (総務), management planning (経営企画), and DX.

External services and specialists that can be used include BPO companies, tax accountants (税理士), certified public accountants (公認会計士), certified social insurance and labor consultants (社会保険労務士), and management consultants (経営コンサルタント).
A capability matrix shows which expert types can typically cover which functions (marked 〇); a note states that some areas may still be handleable depending on the specific provider (※).
When using external services for back-office work, one listed advantage is that the company can cover knowledge and expertise that is insufficient internally.
The section frames merits, demerits, and caution points of outsourcing/using external specialists for back-office functions.

Using external BPO (Business Process Outsourcing) services for back-office operations can supplement internal resource shortages and allow a company to select and use necessary knowledge and resources only when they are needed.

Disadvantages of using external services include communication costs with outside parties, the cost and judgment required to find good partners, the need to decide and draw boundaries between outsourced work and internal work, and the fact that external execution can be more expensive than doing the work internally.

Communication with BPO firms or outside experts requires special caution because they often have only a shallow understanding of the company's internal circumstances and organizational structure; completely handing work over to them (丸投げ) is dangerous.

Internal personnel who understand back-office operations at least to some degree must act as instructors or intermediaries to coordinate with external partners; this coordination requires skills and extra effort.
A company must properly understand the characteristics of its own back-office operations and deliberately design which tasks to outsource (外部化) versus keep internal (内部化).
If that design work is neglected, even spending money to obtain cooperation from external partners will not produce a well-functioning back-office system.
Back office work has traditionally been widely perceived as equivalent to clerical or miscellaneous tasks that anyone can perform, rather than as specialized professional work.

Historically, much of back office work consisted of simple clerical duties (事務職), such as serving tea to clients, photocopying paper documents, filling out vouchers, printing documents, and mailing—often associated with office women in uniforms in older dramas and workplaces.
A notable characteristic of back office operations is a high volume of routine (ルーティン) work combined with a large share of clerical processing tasks.

Many companies historically used a clear internal division of labor: simple clerical work assigned to clerical staff (事務職), highly specialized work assigned to career-track generalists (総合職), and management/executive roles filled by people promoted internally within the department.
This traditional internal division of labor in back office functions has been collapsing.
The old distinction that separated back office work into purely clerical tasks versus specialized professional tasks has been disappearing in recent years.
Environmental changes driving this redefinition include digital transformation (デジタルシフト / IT導入), legal revisions and stronger compliance requirements, and labor shortages.
As a result, back office work itself is being fundamentally reconsidered, and the awareness, mindset, and actual job scope of people in these roles are changing accordingly.
Concrete example of change: accounting clerks who previously spent time creating invoices and performing bookkeeping now see those tasks being replaced or automated by IT systems.
Digitalization has put back-office workers in a position where they must master IT systems themselves in order to survive, because those systems are the cause of workplace change.

Mastering IT systems requires a correct understanding of the underlying business operations: systems excel at executing predetermined processes quickly, efficiently, and accurately, but humans still instruct and correct those processes.
To instruct or modify system processing, staff must accumulate business understanding and related knowledge; simply following a supervisor’s clerical instructions is no longer sufficient.
Digitalization therefore demands that people in back-office roles possess both professional expertise/knowledge and the ability to understand and design correct business processes.

The traditional clerical job (事務職) model—routine work, faithful obedience to a boss, almost no independent judgment—is being replaced as DX/IT automates much of that work; remaining roles shift toward specialized professional work, management, and operational design.
Career goals are changing from internal promotion through routine clerical work toward higher-skill paths that include business-process design and management.
As the nature of management and indirect (staff) departments changes, demand is rising for talent who can carry out ‘back office’ work rather than traditional clerical tasks.
The ability to design work (業務を設計する力) is equivalent to management ability (マネジメント能力), especially in back-office operations.
This ability means understanding business flows and redesigning operations to match environmental changes centered on DX and IT: redefining what work is done, who does it, and when/on what schedule.
In the back office, redefining these elements is close in meaning to performing management.
Visualizing and verbalizing work (業務の見える化・言語化) enables creation of mechanisms and manuals so that anyone performing the work produces the same results.
Role allocation requires correctly understanding the strengths, skills, and know-how of internal talent and external partners, then deciding which work to assign to whom.
Scheduling requires understanding work volume and each person's capabilities, grasping the target deadlines needed to complete deliverables, and deciding how to plan each task.
These activities are essentially the work that middle managers already perform.
Because back-office work contains many standardized/routine tasks, understanding and organizing business flows directly drives operational efficiency.
Therefore back-office staff must acquire at least some of the ability to design work, i.e., management ability.
A core competency in back-office work is the ability to design operations (バックオフィスの業務を設計する力), spanning 経理 (accounting), 人事 (HR), 法務 (legal), 総務 (general affairs), 経営企画 (management planning), and DX.
Business-flow design requires specifying three elements: ① what work is done (どんな業務を), ② who performs it (誰が), and ③ when and on what schedule (いつ・どんなスケジュールで).

Monthly invoicing (請求) example spanning the first five days of the month: Day 1 invoice check (請求書チェック); days 2–3 ARS-related steps; Day 3 invoice completion (請求書の完成); Day 4 invoice creation (請求書の作成) and input into the billing system (請求システムへ入力); Day 5 further invoice check, system input, monthly billing-report check (月次請求レポートのチェック), and transmission to the client (取引先へ).
Roles illustrated include sales-support staff (営業サポート) versus dedicated back-office staff who execute and check the billing workflow.

Future back-office talent should fulfill three criteria: (1) master IT for back-office tasks that DX/IT will replace, (2) broadly understand knowledge and operations up to an intermediate level, and (3) utilize internal and external talent and manage the whole.
The ideal back-office person uses IT skillfully on work that digitalization can substitute, has wide intermediate-level knowledge of many functions, and can orchestrate internal and external people.
As digitalization continues to accelerate, back-office work itself will keep changing; clerical work once dominated the domain, so people in these roles now face an era that demands transformation.

Back office operations (バックオフィス業務) are often grouped under a single term, but the domain is actually wide and each area has a completely different reality. They are divided into large domains according to the roles they should fulfill.
Company management depends on the three essentials of ヒト・モノ・カネ (people, things/goods, and money).

Accounting and finance (経理財務) governs the カネ (money) element. Accounting staff are money experts who manage daily ledgers/books and prepare annual financial statements (決算書) so that the company’s performance results can be communicated both internally and externally.

Accounting and finance also perform fund management from the perspective of whether company funds are circulating sufficiently. This includes making daily cash-flow (資金繰り) forecasts and raising funds from banks and investors, thereby managing the flow of money from both short-term and long-term viewpoints.

Human resources and labor (人事労務) governs the ヒト (people) element. Against the background of a declining working-age population and talent shortages, the purpose of this function is to acquire and develop good talent so that employees can always deliver maximum performance.

HR/labor professionals are experts who take on all people-related work in one place, including talent recruitment (人材採用), education and development (教育開発), design of personnel systems (人事制度づくり), compliance with labor law (労働法の遵守), and social-insurance procedures at joining and leaving (入退社時の社会保険手続き).

Legal affairs (法務) exists so that a company can recognize and control various legal risks related to its business activities. It mainly consists of two types of work: business legal affairs (ビジネス法務) and corporate legal affairs (コーポレート法務).
Business legal affairs involves creating, reviewing, and negotiating contracts when concluding contracts with external customers and suppliers.
Corporate legal affairs manages matters stipulated mainly by the Companies Act, such as shareholders' meetings, board of directors meetings, and registration changes.
In recent years, legal departments have also been strengthening responses to compliance measures such as harassment prevention and internal governance systems.

General affairs (総務) oversees general operations related to company management. Its purpose is to enable the entire company to communicate smoothly and work comfortably by organizing the internal environment and events.

Examples of general affairs work include executing company events, greetings and gifts to business partners, office relocation, and management of OA equipment and supplies. The department acts as an unsung hero (縁の下の力持ち) supporting the organization.
Management planning (経営企画) acts as the hands and feet of management, connecting internal departments so the company can progress toward its management philosophy and vision.

Because management planning supports executives, it has relatively few routine tasks. Representative work includes formulating mid-term management plans and business plans, budget management, promoting M&A, and advancing special projects.
Back-office functions such as HR/labor affairs and accounting exist in every company to a greater or lesser degree.

In a company of a certain size, it is not realistic for one person or one department to cover all back-office work; in practice the work is divided among people and departments, and that division produces the back-office organization.
How a company designs its back-office organization and assigns roles is not uniform; it differs completely from company to company.

Factors that shape back-office organization structure include: (1) the company’s business model—industry, revenue structure, and the speed and magnitude of environmental change; (2) future growth plans—intended growth speed and how the company thinks about investing in people, goods, and money; (3) company-wide organization-design policy and culture—how important back-office functions are considered when those policies and culture are formed.
Role-sharing and organizational patterns can also be examined function-by-function (e.g., by each back-office capability).
Back-office organization design is influenced by company type (large enterprise, SME, or startup) and by the strength of demands from external stakeholders such as investors and banks.
Several patterns exist for designing a back-office organization.
Case 1 — One-person back office: a single employee covers a wide range of back-office work. This pattern is common in SMEs and in seed-to-early-stage startups.
Although the functional domain is broad, one person is limited in volume and depth of coverage, so specialist expertise is typically shallow.
Specialized knowledge is often supplemented by external professionals such as an advisory tax accountant (税理士) and a labor/social-insurance consultant (社労士).
Illustrative structure: management, sales, development and manufacturing functions all rely on a single back-office person.

One back-office organization pattern (Case 2) divides functions by 'people' versus 'money': an HR/labor function that governs people, with a mission of organizational growth and a focus on qualitative, human, and motivational aspects of work, versus an accounting function that governs money, with a mission of business growth and a focus on quantitative, financial, and rational aspects.

In the people-and-money split, department structure is typically built around the larger accounting and HR/labor teams; general affairs, legal, and management-planning functions are then aggregated into one of those two departments.
A second pattern (Case 3) separates strategic-planning functions from management/support functions: units that must directly manage business growth versus units that provide more indirect support.

In the strategic-versus-management split, strategic planning is made independent by pairing management planning with HR (organization and recruitment only; labor affairs are separated), so the unit operates as middle office rather than purely back office.

Back-office organization can split functions into an 'offensive' (攻め) department that is given roles and is more conscious of business growth, versus a 'defensive' (守り) department specialized in risk management.
Concentrating accounting (経理), general affairs (総務), labor affairs (労務), and legal (法務) functions into a management-control (経営管理) department creates a risk-management-focused defensive unit.

Separating management planning (経営企画) from management control is one organizational pattern, with the former more growth-oriented and the latter more control/risk-oriented, under a management layer that also oversees sales, development, and manufacturing.
Case 4 pattern: organize a separate department for each back-office function rather than combining them.
In medium-sized and larger companies where back-office headcount is growing, functional department organization is common.

Around a company size of 100 employees total and a back-office team of 10–15 people, independent departments typically appear: accounting department (経理部), HR department (人事部), general affairs department (総務部), legal department (法務部), and management planning department (経営企画部).
Once those specialized back-office departments exist independently, they advance work while coordinating and collaborating with one another.
Back-office operations (バックオフィス業務) span accounting (経理), human resources (人事), legal affairs (法務), general affairs (総務), corporate/management planning (経営企画), and DX (digital transformation).
One organizational pattern is dividing departments by function (機能ごとに部署を分ける), illustrated with parallel business units (事業部) labeled A, B, and C.
Back office organization design is equivalent to the formation of back office culture.
Overall design policy for a back office organization has many variations from company to company, so organizational design methods other than the example cases also exist.
How the back office organization is designed determines the functions required of the back office and the value it provides, and this in turn gives rise to the culture of back office members.
Back-office work cannot be treated as one uniform category: it is typically divided into HR/labor, accounting, legal, general affairs, and management planning, and each domain has a different nature.
Understanding back-office domains by shared characteristics (rather than looking at each function in isolation) is useful for organization design and for assessing one's own capabilities.

A practical way to understand the domains is to map them on two major axes (a four-quadrant view). The page illustrates domains such as finance/accounting, HR/recruitment, and management planning, plus applied capability.
Mapping viewpoint 1: Place yourself in one of the four quadrants according to where you are suited. Do not try to cover everything; apply priorities (メリハリ) and consider using external specialists.

Mapping viewpoint 2: Beyond domain-specific work, add value that is common across back office: speed and flexibility; ability to build mechanisms and understand business processes; IT literacy, and similar skills.
Back-office work can be classified along two axes: the core ability required to perform the work, and the method/process emphasized in decision-making.
The first axis of required ability is split into 知識力 (knowledge power) and 応用力 (application power).

知識力 is the ability to construct work on the premise of domain knowledge. Quality and performance of the work change depending on whether one possesses that knowledge. Accounting is knowledge-power-heavy: without accounting standards and bookkeeping, even a person with strong raw intellect cannot do the job. Typical accounting staff first study bookkeeping or accumulate equivalent knowledge on the job before they can work independently.

応用力 is the ability to construct work by combining knowledge and experience from multiple domains, connecting dots into a surface. Management planning is application-power-heavy: one must know (or look up) a wide range of business topics—market size, the company’s strengths, talent, laws, etc.—and combine them to produce competent work.
The second axis of decision-making method/process is split into 調整・コミュニケーション (coordination/communication) and 論理性 (logic).

Coordination/communication work produces outcomes that vary greatly with the company’s background, industry, competitors, and historical context. Creating new evaluation or wage regulations in HR is an example: the content must reflect employees’ mindsets and the company’s accumulated history, so one must understand emotional/ambiguous factors and obtain consensus rather than simply writing a “correct” rule.

Logic work yields answers by rationally connecting cause-and-effect relationships. Legal work, especially business-contract negotiation, is logic-heavy: by thoroughly thinking through the company’s own strategy and purpose and understanding the other party’s purpose, win-win contract terms can be constructed. Logical thinking and understanding/organizing business structure are therefore paramount.
These two-axis characteristics of each back-office function should be used as the basis for organization design and personnel placement.

The four domains of back-office work represent the very directions in which talent grows. No one is a “superman” who possesses all of them; every person has a tendency or characteristic of being strong in one or more of these four areas.
The relative importance of different back-office functions changes according to a company’s business model and growth stage.
It is important to understand the individuality and characteristics of each back-office person and to staff and compose the back-office team in accordance with the company’s situation.
Do not try to fill every required headcount perfectly. When back-office talent is insufficient, using BPO (business-process outsourcing) firms or specialists is an effective means.
When the back-office organization has been designed and talent with the needed skills is lacking, leveraging external resources is a valid approach.

Some managers insist on assembling a complete in-house back-office function and work hard to gather talent, but back-office organization-building should proceed in step with the company’s growth stage and current business environment.

Finding, by one’s own efforts alone, all the talent needed to neatly fill required functions is difficult. Because each back-office member has a different desired growth direction and a different growth speed, it is more realistic and more successfully managed to change the structure and the division of duties flexibly.
In modern management, rapid and flexible response to changes in the business environment is an indispensable element.

Digitalization is one of the factors that has advanced the transformation of back-office operations, and the back office's ability to respond to management-environment changes greatly affects its operational performance.

Back-office activities such as management planning (creating business strategy), HR (recruiting talent), accounting (conducting performance analysis), general affairs (facilitating communication), and legal (examining business schemes) are indispensable foundational activities for a company's growth and development and become the company's inherent strength (地力).
These operational methods must constantly be reviewed from a zero base in accordance with changes in the management environment.

When a back-office organization runs these activities, it should hold high ideals/policy so that members adapt to change, grow spontaneously and autonomously, mutually raise performance, and can exert a positive influence on the front office and management team.
A company with such a back office can be imagined as one that overcomes any environmental change or hardship and continues to develop.

For the back office to run the organization and contribute to corporate development, a Back Office Policy (バックオフィス・ポリシー) — the vision for the back office — is necessary; it functions as the compass that unifies the back office.

Not limited to the back office, when a company formulates management strategy, establishing and thoroughly communicating mission and vision as the most important concept before strategy and organization-building is an iron rule of management.
A concrete example of a Back Office Policy created at a company the author was involved with is presented as an illustration.

Back-office corporate policies illustrated on this page are 攻めて守る (offense/defense: both attacking improvement and protecting operations), Versatile, ゼロベース思考 (zero-based thinking), and プロフェッショナリズム (professionalism).

Don'ts of back-office work include treating routines as inescapable busywork while complaining they are boring, asking why you personally must do a given task, watching colleagues' effort with an outsider/spectator attitude, claiming the work is unrelated to what you want to do, refusing change because 'last time you said X so don't change it,' copying what a person or another company does without original thought, spending half a day worrying with zero output, making other-blame excuses ('no time / I was doing something else'), restricting communication to only email or only chat or only verbal, and either charging ahead without consultation or glossing over unclear ('モヤっとした') points.

Do's of back-office work include temporarily dropping routines when medium- to long-term structural change matters, asking how a routine can be solved by a mechanism/system, discussing with colleagues whether something large or interesting can be done, recognizing that work will eventually return to you, transferring a method from one job to another, checking whether the background has changed since a prior conclusion, researching others' statements to form a hypothesis, using other-company examples and others' opinions to take one step beyond your own limits, taking self-responsibility ('sorry, the cause this time was XX'), using any communication channel that solves the problem rather than sticking to one medium, consulting immediately when something is unclear, and explicitly recognizing your own strengths and weaknesses.

The mindset contrast is other-responsibility vs. self-responsibility, rigid communication vs. problem-first communication, and routine-as-fate vs. routine-as-something-to-systematize or occasionally set aside for bigger structural work.

There is no absolute right or wrong in what kind of back-office policy a company creates. The important point is to establish some criteria the team should value, thereby showing the 'correct path' within that team.

A back-office policy can be expressed as Do's & Don'ts (behaviors that should be praised versus those that should not). These give members shared right/wrong guidance for the situations they encounter while working together.
Even when the company as a whole has goals, back office still needs its own policy because it has unique challenges that must be overcome for the function to unite as one.

Challenge 1 — Different domain characteristics and different organizational-design methods: Each back-office area has a different nature of work, so the people who work there also differ. When people doing dissimilar work and possessing different personalities must unite, a single large common goal is required. One shared goal generates team feeling and a sense of belonging.

Challenge 2 — Goals are hard to set and hard to feel: Back office rarely generates revenue itself and is often called a cost center (a department that incurs costs rather than producing revenue). Individual and team goals therefore tend to be unquantifiable or vague. A clear policy, together with an explicit sense of fulfillment toward its achievement, can positively affect growth goals and career formation for back-office staff.

Challenge 3 — Demonstrating presence as an important company function: In companies that undervalue back office, management-control functions in particular fail to develop, and growth speed plus the ability to respond to environmental change tend to weaken.
Back-office capabilities are especially important in high-stakes situations such as formulating business plans, fundraising, IPO preparation, and M&A.

Creating a clear back-office policy helps communicate internally and externally that the back office is a strategically important management function, which strengthens its presence and enables more dynamic execution of corporate strategy.
A back-office policy’s specific content varies by company-wide or function-specific direction, but good policies share several design principles.

Link the policy to company-wide strategy: set goals so that the back office’s ideal actions always produce a positive impact on the front office and overall management; avoid goals that conflict with the company’s mission, vision, or management strategy.

Combine passion and logic in the vision: design organizational goals that mix vivid, on-the-ground understanding of the front office and management with the calm, supporting perspective needed for the whole organization.

Express the company’s unique character (“rashisa”): because members will interpret goals slightly differently, state them in simple, powerful language so they are easy to understand, generate empathy, and build team unity.

Have leaders who possess deep knowledge and experience in both back-office operations and management: such a leader can develop the back-office team into the company’s true backbone, solve complex corporate issues, and serve as a suitable vessel for instilling the vision.
Back-office operations (バックオフィス業務) include numerous periodic tasks that are mandated by laws and company rules and must be performed on a regular basis.

When mastering specific back-office tasks, it is essential to understand the framework in which each task is performed by focusing on three key points: the schedule, the submission/reporting destinations, and the documents that must be created and submitted.

Back-office task schedules fall into three categories: tasks that must be performed on an annual basis (年間単位), tasks that must be performed on a monthly basis (1カ月単位), and tasks that must be performed whenever they arise on a daily basis (日々発生するたびに).

Submission and reporting destinations for back-office work include government offices such as tax offices (税務署) and labor standards inspection offices (労働基準監督署), business counterparts such as suppliers and customers, and funding sources such as shareholders and financial institutions.
Required documents must be prepared and submitted, and supporting attachments must not be forgotten.

Understanding the schedule is especially important for back-office work because there are many periodic tasks; these should be scheduled so that work can be carried out in a planned, systematic manner.
Back-office work often cannot be processed independently within the back-office team; most tasks require gathering information from employees in other company departments.
Regular internal back-office meetings should be held to visualize (見える化) each task’s deadlines, because otherwise omissions and mistakes tend to increase.
Team members should divide responsibilities and confirm schedules that include time for advance preparation plus coordination and handoffs with other departments, then act ahead of time.
Annual back-office tasks (as opposed to monthly ones) frequently have legally mandated deadlines and are therefore more important; grasp the yearly schedule in advance.

Accounting-related annual tasks often shift depending on the company’s fiscal year-end month, so always confirm your own company’s closing month (the book’s example schedule assumes a March fiscal year-end).

Back-office department busy and idle periods (繁閑) are determined by the annual schedule. Accounting (経理) and HR/labor (人事労務) work often has legally mandated response periods, so peak and slow seasons are relatively easy to forecast.
Plan member vacation timing and overtime forecasts in advance while considering overall departmental workload, because legal deadlines make busy/idle cycles predictable.

Monthly back-office work includes both legally required tasks and company-specific deadlines (e.g., issuing invoices to clients, internal performance reports to executives and management). Firmly grasp the company’s own rules and due dates.

Example monthly back-office schedule items: new-hire onboarding procedures (入社手続対応), payroll calculation (給与計算の実施), supplier payment transfers (仕入先支払先への振込, often in the second week), and accounting/finance (経理財務) tasks.

Compared with annual operations, many back-office tasks have smaller individual volumes and high routine/repetitive character; rather than estimating time for each task from scratch every time, the key is to assign roles as much as possible and to build systems and manuals so the work can be performed efficiently.
Financial closing (決算業務) is one of the highest-weight tasks among back-office operations.
Even after extensive internal and external experience (listed and unlisted companies, audit firms, tax accountants), closing still feels consistently difficult (“決算って大変だなあ……”).

Until recently, closing season commonly meant expected holiday work, overtime until the last train, and taxi rides home; in large firms, work is divided by account or issue, yet if any one person is unfinished the whole close cannot be completed, so teams often cover for one another on holidays.
Closing procedures look routine but actually change a little every year because of revisions to accounting standards (会計基準) and business developments, so they cannot be handled mechanically.
Successfully completing the close produces a strong sense of achievement.
Work-style reform (働き方改革) and IT have reduced individual workload, yet closing remains a major rite of passage for an accounting professional to become fully competent.
経理財務の業務とは一言で言えば「お金」に関する業務である。ただし会社が行う活動のほとんどにお金が関係するため、それだけでは何でも経理財務の仕事になってしまう。
経理財務の仕事は分類して捉えることが重要で、その分類がそのまま実務内容や部署分けにつながる。まずこれらの分類を理解することから始める。
経理財務の仕事の主な分類：単体決算（帳簿作成／会計方針、単体決算作成・報告）、連結決算（連結決算作成・報告）、資金関連（資金調達、入金／支払管理）、全体（予算／中期経営計画、業績分析）、現場（営業所・工場などでのKPI管理、投資意思決定）、税務（税務申告、税金対策）。

Minimum points that anyone involved in accounting and finance (経理財務) must understand: (1) understanding of laws and rules (法令・ルールの理解), (2) understanding of stakeholders (ステークホルダーの理解), and (3) understanding of the business (ビジネスの理解).

The first key point for accounting and finance work is understanding relevant laws and rules, including the Companies Act (会社法), the Financial Instruments and Exchange Act (金融商品取引法), accounting standards (会計基準), and tax law (税法).
